name: Low Earth orbit (400 km)
description: Close to Earth, so images are sharp and radio links are easy. You spend over a third of each orbit in shadow, so the battery works hard.

name: Space-station orbit (420 km, 51.6°)
description: The same tilted orbit as the International Space Station. Easy to reach, but it never passes over the polar regions.

name: Sun-synchronous orbit (550 km)
description: Passes over every place at the same local time each day: ideal for comparing images over months. Covers the whole globe.

name: Dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit (600 km)
description: Rides the line between day and night, so the solar panels almost never see shadow. The ground below is in twilight, which is poor for photos.

name: Geostationary orbit (35,786 km)
description: Hovers over one spot of the equator and stays in constant contact with one ground station. Far away, so images are blurry and radiation is high.

name: Low lunar orbit (50 km)
description: Skims the Moon for the sharpest views. The Moon's uneven gravity makes this orbit unstable, so it costs extra fuel to keep.

name: Low lunar orbit (100 km)
description: A classic mapping orbit around the Moon: close enough for detailed maps, high enough to be stable for a while.

name: Polar lunar orbit (100 km)
description: Passes over both lunar poles, where water ice hides in craters that never see sunlight. Covers the whole Moon over a month.

name: Elliptical lunar orbit (3,000 km average)
description: A long, stretched orbit that is cheap to enter and rarely in shadow, but the spacecraft spends most of its time far from the surface.

name: Low Mars orbit (300 km)
description: A close orbit for detailed science. Entering it takes a big braking burn after a 7-month cruise.

name: Mars sun-synchronous orbit (400 km)
description: Crosses each region at the same local time, like Earth's sun-synchronous orbits. The standard choice for Mars mapping missions.

name: Elliptical Mars orbit (300 × 33,000 km)
description: Cheap to enter, but the spacecraft is close to Mars for only a short part of each orbit.

name: High circular Mars orbit (6,000 km)
description: A high, stable orbit with short eclipses. Good for watching the atmosphere and weather, poor for close-up imaging.
